questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Essentials of partnership
questions.stem: Girish manages Kapoor Trading Co. under a written contract that entitles him to 20% of the firm's annual profits as remuneration. He takes no part in decisions binding the firm and cannot contract on its behalf. Is Girish a partner?

options.text: Yes — sharing profits under a contract is by itself conclusive proof of partnership
options.explanation: Section 4 makes profit-sharing an essential ingredient, but the courts and the Act treat it as evidence only. A creditor, a widow of a deceased partner and a manager may all receive a share of profits without being partners.

options.text: Yes — because his entitlement is fixed by a written contract rather than by custom
options.explanation: The form of the agreement is irrelevant. A partnership can be oral and a non-partner's entitlement can be written; what matters is the relationship the agreement creates.

options.text: No — he shares profits but there is no mutual agency, so the relation of partnership does not arise
options.explanation: Correct. Section 4 requires a business carried on by all or any of them 'acting for all'. That phrase is the mutual-agency test: each partner must be able to bind the firm and be bound by the others. Girish cannot bind the firm, so he is an employee paid by reference to profits.

options.text: No — because a partner must contribute capital and Girish has contributed none
options.explanation: Contribution of capital is not an essential of partnership. A working partner who brings only skill is still a partner, provided mutual agency exists.

questions.sourceRef: Indian Partnership Act 1932, s.4 — mutual agency is the decisive test

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Essentials of partnership
questions.stem: Which of the following is a partnership within the meaning of the Indian Partnership Act 1932?

options.text: Two friends who jointly buy a shop, run it as a general store and share the profits equally
options.explanation: Correct. All three essentials are present: an agreement between persons, a business carried on for profit, and mutual agency — each of them runs the store on behalf of both. Sharing the profits completes the picture.

options.text: The members of a Hindu Undivided Family carrying on the family's ancestral cloth business
options.explanation: A HUF business is not a partnership. Its members become co-parceners by birth, not by agreement, and partnership must arise from contract.

options.text: Three cousins who inherit a warehouse and share the rent it earns in equal shares
options.explanation: This is co-ownership, not partnership. There is no business being carried on — only a jointly owned asset producing income.

options.text: A club whose members pool subscriptions to run a library for their own use
options.explanation: There is no business carried on with a view to profit. A members' club is a not-for-profit association, not a firm.

questions.sourceRef: Indian Partnership Act 1932, s.4 — agreement, business, mutual agency

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Rules in the absence of a deed
questions.stem: Two partners have no partnership deed at all. Which of the following statements about the year's accounts is CORRECT?

options.text: Profits are divided in the ratio of the partners' capitals, and interest on capital is allowed at 6% p.a.
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong. The Act divides profits equally, whatever the capitals, and allows no interest on capital at all when the deed is silent.

options.text: A partner who works full time in the business is entitled to reasonable remuneration for his services
options.explanation: Section 13(a) says the opposite: a partner is not entitled to any remuneration for taking part in the conduct of the business unless the deed provides for it.

options.text: Interest on drawings is charged at 6% p.a. so that a partner who withdraws more is not favoured
options.explanation: There is no such rule. Interest on drawings is charged only if the deed provides for it; with no deed, no interest on drawings is charged at any rate.

options.text: Profits and losses are shared equally, and a partner who advances money beyond his agreed capital is entitled to interest at 6% p.a. on that advance
options.explanation: Correct. Section 13(b) gives equal shares of profits and equal contribution to losses regardless of capitals, and s.13(d) entitles a partner who makes an advance beyond his agreed capital to interest at six per cent per annum on that advance.

readLink.label: Read: Rules when the deed is silent, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Indian Partnership Act 1932, s.13(a), (b), (d)

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Rules in the absence of a deed
questions.stem: Ravi and Sunil are partners with capitals of ₹8,00,000 and ₹4,00,000. There is no partnership deed. On 1 April 2025 Sunil advanced a further ₹3,00,000 to the firm as a loan. The profit for the year ended 31 March 2026, before anything in respect of that loan, is ₹4,98,000. The total amount credited to Sunil for the year (interest plus share of profit) is:

options.explanation: This allows no interest on Sunil's advance and simply halves ₹4,98,000. But s.13(d) gives a partner 6% p.a. on money advanced beyond his agreed capital even when the deed is silent — that right comes from the Act, not from the deed.

Correct. Interest on the advance = 3,00,000 × 6% = ₹18,000, which is a CHARGE and is deducted before divisible profit. Divisible profit = 4,98,000 − 18,000 = ₹4,80,000, shared EQUALLY because the deed is silent = ₹2,40,000 each. Sunil is credited 2,40,000 + 18,000 = ₹2,58,000.

This divides the ₹4,80,000 in the capital ratio 8:4, giving Sunil ₹1,60,000 plus ₹18,000 interest. Section 13(b) requires equal shares when the deed is silent, however unequal the capitals — this is the most common error in the whole chapter.
This deducts the ₹18,000 interest as a charge but then forgets to credit it to Sunil. The interest leaves the firm's profit and lands in Sunil's account; it cannot simply disappear.

readLink.label: Read: Rules when the deed is silent, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: s.13(d) 6% on advances (a charge) + s.13(b) equal shares

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Rules in the absence of a deed
questions.stem: A partnership deed allows interest on capital at 10% p.a. In the year ended 31 March 2026 the firm made a net loss. What interest on capital is allowed?

options.text: None — interest on capital is payable only out of profits, so in a loss year it is not allowed at all
options.explanation: Correct. Section 13(c) provides that where a partner is entitled to interest on capital, such interest is payable only out of profits. Interest on capital is an appropriation, and there is nothing to appropriate in a loss year; allowing it would only enlarge the loss.

options.text: The full 10%, because the deed is a contract and overrides the Act
options.explanation: The deed can create the entitlement but cannot change its character. Interest on capital remains an appropriation of profit, and s.13(c) confines it to profits.

options.text: 10% for the part of the year up to the date the loss was first identified
options.explanation: There is no such apportionment rule. The test is applied to the year's result as a whole.

options.text: 6% instead of 10%, the Act's rate replacing the deed's rate in a loss year
options.explanation: The 6% rate in s.13(d) belongs to a partner's ADVANCE, not to capital, and it applies whether or not there is a profit. It has nothing to do with interest on capital.

readLink.label: Read: Rules when the deed is silent, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Indian Partnership Act 1932, s.13(c) — interest on capital payable only out of profits

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Charge vs appropriation
questions.stem: Which one of the following is a CHARGE against profit rather than an appropriation of profit?

options.text: Interest on a partner's capital allowed by the deed at 8% p.a.
options.explanation: Interest on capital rewards a partner as an OWNER. It is an appropriation, debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and possible only if there is a profit.

options.text: A monthly salary payable to the working partner under the deed
options.explanation: A partner's salary is a reward for being an owner-manager and is an appropriation. Only an employee's or manager's salary is a charge.

options.text: Rent payable to a partner for his own building occupied by the firm as a godown
options.explanation: Correct. Here the partner is dealing with the firm as an OUTSIDER — a landlord. Rent is a normal business expense, debited to the Profit and Loss Account before net profit is struck, and it is payable whether or not the firm makes a profit.

options.text: The annual transfer to the firm's General Reserve required by the deed
options.explanation: A transfer to reserve is a setting-aside of profit already earned — an appropriation. It cannot be made in a loss year.

questions.sourceRef: Charge = P&L Account, payable regardless of profit; appropriation = division of profit

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Charge vs appropriation
questions.stem: Meera and Nita share profits 3:2. The firm's profit for the year ended 31 March 2026, before any of the following, is ₹7,50,000. Meera is paid rent of ₹15,000 per month for her building used as the firm's godown. Nita's loan of ₹4,00,000 has been outstanding for the whole year and the deed says nothing about interest on it. The deed allows Meera a salary of ₹10,000 per month. The divisible profit is:

options.explanation: This omits the interest on Nita's loan because the deed is silent. Section 13(d) supplies 6% p.a. on a partner's advance precisely when the deed does not — 4,00,000 × 6% = ₹24,000, a charge.

Correct. Rent to a partner ₹1,80,000 (15,000 × 12) and interest on Nita's loan ₹24,000 (4,00,000 × 6%) are CHARGES, deducted before net profit: 7,50,000 − 1,80,000 − 24,000 = ₹5,46,000. Meera's salary ₹1,20,000 (10,000 × 12) is an APPROPRIATION: 5,46,000 − 1,20,000 = ₹4,26,000 divisible.

This leaves the rent out on the view that a partner cannot charge his own firm. He can: when a partner lets his property to the firm he acts as a landlord, and the rent is an ordinary business expense.
This is the net profit AFTER the two charges but BEFORE Meera's salary. The salary is an appropriation and must still come out before the balance is divisible.

questions.sourceRef: Rent to a partner and interest on a partner's loan are charges; partner's salary is an appropriation

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
questions.stem: Which pair of items appears on the CREDIT side of the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account?

options.text: Interest on capital and partners' salaries
options.explanation: Both are debits — they are appropriations taken out of the available profit.

options.text: Net profit brought down and the transfer to General Reserve
options.explanation: Net profit b/d is indeed a credit, but the transfer to reserve is a debit: it takes profit away before the balance is divided.

options.text: Interest on drawings and the share of profit transferred to partners
options.explanation: Interest on drawings is a credit, but the share of profit transferred to the partners is the debit that closes the account.

options.text: Net profit brought down from the Profit and Loss Account, and interest on drawings
options.explanation: Correct. The account is credited with the profit available for division and with interest charged to the partners on their drawings; everything else — interest on capital, salary, commission, reserve and the partners' shares — sits on the debit side.

questions.sourceRef: Appropriation Account: credits = net profit b/d + interest on drawings

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
questions.stem: P and Q are partners. Net profit for the year ended 31 March 2026, after all charges, is ₹8,00,000. The deed provides interest on capital of ₹60,000 to P and ₹40,000 to Q, a salary of ₹1,50,000 to Q, interest on drawings of ₹6,000 from P and ₹4,000 from Q, and a transfer of ₹80,000 to the General Reserve. The divisible profit is:

options.explanation: This DEDUCTS the ₹10,000 of interest on drawings instead of adding it. Interest on drawings is money the partners owe the firm, so it increases the profit available for division — it sits on the credit side.

Correct. Credits = 8,00,000 + 10,000 (interest on drawings 6,000 + 4,000) = ₹8,10,000. Debits = 1,00,000 (interest on capital 60,000 + 40,000) + 1,50,000 (Q's salary) + 80,000 (reserve) = ₹3,30,000. Divisible profit = 8,10,000 − 3,30,000 = ₹4,80,000.
This omits the ₹80,000 transfer to General Reserve. A transfer to reserve is an appropriation and must be debited before the balance is divided among the partners.
This omits Q's salary of ₹1,50,000. A partner's salary provided for by the deed is an appropriation and is debited to this account.

questions.sourceRef: Divisible profit = Net profit + interest on drawings − interest on capital − salary − reserve

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
questions.stem: A and B have capitals of ₹6,00,000 and ₹4,00,000. The deed allows interest on capital at 10% p.a. as an appropriation of profit. The profit for the year ended 31 March 2026, after all charges, is only ₹75,000. The interest on capital actually allowed to A is:

options.explanation: Correct. The full entitlement is A ₹60,000 and B ₹40,000, a total of ₹1,00,000, but only ₹75,000 of profit exists. The available profit is distributed in the RATIO OF THE APPROPRIATIONS CLAIMED, 60,000 : 40,000 = 6 : 4, so A receives 75,000 × 6/10 = ₹45,000 and B ₹30,000.
This allows the full entitlement. Interest on capital is an appropriation, so it cannot exceed the profit available — allowing ₹1,00,000 out of ₹75,000 would manufacture a loss.
This splits the ₹75,000 equally. The shortfall is shared in the ratio of the amounts CLAIMED (6:4 here), not equally and not in the profit-sharing ratio.
This is B's figure — the 6:4 ratio has been applied the wrong way round. A has the larger capital and therefore the larger claim.

questions.sourceRef: Insufficient profit: appropriations allowed in the ratio of the amounts claimed

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Interest on capital
questions.stem: Kiran's capital on 1 April 2025 was ₹5,00,000. He introduced a further ₹2,40,000 on 1 August 2025 and permanently withdrew ₹1,20,000 of capital on 1 January 2026. The deed allows interest on capital at 9% p.a. Interest on Kiran's capital for the year ended 31 March 2026 is:

options.explanation: This charges 9% on the opening capital only and ignores both the introduction and the withdrawal. Interest runs on the capital actually employed through the year.
This applies 9% to the CLOSING capital of ₹6,20,000 (5,00,000 + 2,40,000 − 1,20,000). The closing figure was in use only for the last three months, so it cannot carry a full year's interest.
This gives credit for the ₹2,40,000 introduced but ignores the ₹1,20,000 permanently withdrawn. A withdrawal of capital reduces the capital employed for the rest of the year.

questions.sourceRef: Interest on capital runs on the capital actually employed, month by month

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Interest on capital
questions.stem: Anand's capital account is kept on the fluctuating method and stood at ₹7,22,000 on 31 March 2026. During the year he introduced ₹1,00,000 of additional capital on 1 April 2025, was credited with ₹1,80,000 as his share of profit and ₹36,000 as interest on capital, and withdrew ₹90,000, on which interest of ₹4,000 was charged. His capital on 1 April 2025 was:

options.explanation: This deducts the drawings and adds back the interest on drawings — both signs are reversed. Drawings REDUCED the closing balance, so they must be added back when you work backwards.
This works back through every item except the ₹36,000 interest on capital. Interest credited during the year increased the closing balance and must be removed on the way back.
This forgets the ₹1,00,000 of additional capital introduced. Fresh capital also swelled the closing balance and must be taken out.

Correct. Opening capital = Closing 7,22,000 − additional 1,00,000 − share of profit 1,80,000 − interest on capital 36,000 + drawings 90,000 + interest on drawings 4,000 = ₹5,00,000. Check: interest on capital = 6% of (5,00,000 + 1,00,000 introduced on the first day) = ₹36,000, which matches the figure given.

questions.sourceRef: Working back from closing to opening capital under the fluctuating method

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Interest on drawings
questions.stem: Deepa withdrew ₹8,000 at the BEGINNING of every month during the year ended 31 March 2026. The deed charges interest on drawings at 12% p.a. The interest is:

options.explanation: This uses 5.5 months, the average period for drawings made at the END of each month. Money drawn at the beginning of a month is out of the firm longer, so the period is 6.5 months.
This uses 6 months, the average period for drawings made in the MIDDLE of each month (also the convention when no date is given). The stem says beginning of the month.

Correct. Total drawings = 8,000 × 12 = ₹96,000. Equal monthly drawings at the beginning of the month carry an average period of 6.5 months: (12 + 1) ÷ 2 = 6.5. Interest = 96,000 × 12% × 6.5/12 = ₹6,240.
This charges a full 12 months on the whole ₹96,000. Only the first instalment was out for almost the whole year; the last was out for a month.

questions.sourceRef: Equal monthly drawings at the beginning: average period 6.5 months

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Interest on drawings
questions.stem: Farhan withdrew ₹15,000 at the beginning of each quarter during the year ended 31 March 2026. Interest on drawings is charged at 10% p.a. The interest is:

options.explanation: This uses 4.5 months, the average period for drawings made at the END of each quarter. Beginning-of-quarter drawings are out three months longer on average.

Correct. Total drawings = 15,000 × 4 = ₹60,000. The first quarter's drawing is out 12 months and the last 3 months, so the average period = (12 + 3) ÷ 2 = 7.5 months. Interest = 60,000 × 10% × 7.5/12 = ₹3,750.
This uses 6 months, the middle-of-quarter (and no-date) average period. The stem specifies the beginning of each quarter.
This charges a full year's interest on the whole ₹60,000, ignoring that the money went out in four instalments spread across the year.

questions.sourceRef: Equal quarterly drawings at the beginning: average period 7.5 months

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Interest on drawings
questions.stem: Gita's drawings during the year ended 31 March 2026 were: ₹20,000 on 1 May 2025, ₹30,000 on 1 August 2025, ₹15,000 on 1 December 2025 and ₹25,000 on 1 February 2026. Interest on drawings is charged at 9% p.a. Using the product method, the interest is:

options.explanation: This takes a flat 6 months on the total drawings of ₹90,000. The 6-month shortcut applies only when the drawings are equal and evenly spaced, or when no dates are given at all — here the dates and the amounts are both irregular.
This charges a full 12 months on the whole ₹90,000. Interest runs only from the date of each drawing to the year end.
This counts months from 1 April to the date of each drawing (1, 4, 8 and 10) instead of from the date of drawing to the year end. The period that matters is how long the money was OUT of the firm.

questions.sourceRef: Product method: interest = total rupee-month products × rate ÷ 12

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Interest on drawings
questions.stem: A deed charges interest on drawings at 12% p.a. The trial balance shows only 'Drawings — ₹1,20,000' with no dates and no pattern. What period is taken?

options.text: 12 months, because the drawings are presumed to have been made on the first day of the year
options.explanation: There is no such presumption, and it would produce the harshest possible charge on facts the question has not given.

options.text: Nil, because interest cannot be computed without dates, so no interest is charged
options.explanation: The deed's provision is not defeated by silence in the trial balance; the convention below supplies the missing period.

options.text: 6 months, the accepted convention when the dates of drawings are not given
options.explanation: Correct. Where only the total drawings are known, interest is taken for an average period of six months — the midpoint of the year. Interest here would be 1,20,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹7,200.

options.text: 6.5 months, the same average period as equal drawings at the beginning of each month
options.explanation: 6.5 months applies only when the question actually tells you the drawings were equal and made at the beginning of each month. With no information at all, the neutral midpoint of 6 months is used.

questions.sourceRef: Convention: drawings with no dates carry an average period of 6 months

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Fixed and fluctuating capitals
questions.stem: A firm keeps its partners' capitals on the FIXED capital method. Which item is recorded in the Capital Account rather than in the Current Account?

options.text: The partner's share of the year's profit
options.explanation: Under the fixed method the share of profit is credited to the Current Account. The Capital Account would otherwise change every year, which is exactly what the method avoids.

options.text: Interest allowed on the partner's capital
options.explanation: Interest on capital is credited to the Current Account. It is computed ON the capital but it is not itself capital.

options.text: Additional capital permanently introduced by the partner during the year
options.explanation: Correct. The Capital Account moves only when capital is actually brought in or permanently withdrawn. Everything else — interest on capital, salary, commission, share of profit or loss, drawings and interest on drawings — passes through the Current Account.

options.text: The partner's drawings against his expected share of profit
options.explanation: Drawings against profit are debited to the Current Account. Only a permanent withdrawal of capital touches the Capital Account.

questions.sourceRef: Fixed capital method: Capital A/c moves only on introduction or permanent withdrawal of capital

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Fixed and fluctuating capitals
questions.stem: Under the fixed capital method, a partner's Current Account shows a DEBIT balance at the year end. How is it presented in the balance sheet?

options.text: Deducted from the General Reserve on the liabilities side
options.explanation: A partner's account is never set against the firm's reserves. The reserve belongs to all the partners collectively.

options.text: On the ASSETS side, because the partner owes that amount to the firm
options.explanation: Correct. A debit balance on a Current Account means the partner has drawn more than the firm owed him, so the firm has a claim against him — an asset. A credit balance would appear on the liabilities side alongside the capitals.

options.text: Added to the partner's Capital Account, which is then shown net on the liabilities side
options.explanation: That would defeat the whole point of the fixed method, under which the Capital Account stays unchanged. The two accounts are presented separately.

options.text: It cannot arise, because a Current Account can never show a debit balance
options.explanation: It is the Capital Account under the fixed method that normally cannot go into debit. The Current Account can and often does, precisely because drawings run through it.

questions.sourceRef: Debit balance of a Current Account is an asset of the firm

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Guarantee of minimum profit
questions.stem: A, B and C share profits 3:2:1. C is guaranteed a minimum share of ₹1,00,000 per year, any deficiency being borne by A and B in their mutual profit-sharing ratio. The profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 is ₹4,80,000. B's share of profit is:

options.explanation: This is B's normal share before the guarantee is applied. C's normal share falls short of his guarantee, so a deficiency does arise and B must bear part of it.
This splits the ₹20,000 deficiency equally between A and B. The stem says it is borne in their MUTUAL profit-sharing ratio, which is 3:2, not equally.
This applies the ratio the wrong way round, making B bear ₹12,000 and A ₹8,000. B's ratio against A is 2 against 3, so B bears the smaller share.

questions.sourceRef: Deficiency borne by the guaranteeing partners in their mutual ratio

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Guarantee of minimum profit
questions.stem: X, Y and Z share profits 5:3:2. Z is guaranteed a minimum of ₹1,20,000 per year BY X ALONE. The profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 is ₹5,00,000. X's share of profit is:

options.explanation: Correct. Normal shares are X ₹2,50,000, Y ₹1,50,000 and Z ₹1,00,000. Z falls ₹20,000 short of his guarantee, and because X alone gave the guarantee the whole ₹20,000 comes off X's share: 2,50,000 − 20,000 = ₹2,30,000. Y is untouched at ₹1,50,000.
This ignores the guarantee altogether. Z's normal share of ₹1,00,000 is below the guaranteed ₹1,20,000, so the shortfall must be made good.
This spreads the ₹20,000 deficiency over X and Y in 5:3, charging X ₹12,500. The guarantee was given by X alone, so Y bears nothing.
This splits the deficiency equally between X and Y, charging X ₹10,000. Again, only the guaranteeing partner bears it.

questions.sourceRef: Guarantee by one partner alone: the whole deficiency falls on him

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Past adjustments
questions.stem: D, E and F are partners with FIXED capitals of ₹5,00,000, ₹4,00,000 and ₹1,00,000, sharing profits 2:2:1. After the accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026 were closed it was discovered that interest on capital at 8% p.a., which the deed requires, had not been allowed. The single adjusting entry is:

options.text: F's Capital A/c Dr ₹8,000; To D's Capital A/c ₹8,000
options.explanation: Correct. Interest that should have been credited: D ₹40,000, E ₹32,000, F ₹8,000 = ₹80,000. Had it been allowed, the divisible profit would have been ₹80,000 lower, borne 2:2:1 = D ₹32,000, E ₹32,000, F ₹16,000. Net: D +₹8,000, E nil, F −₹8,000. So F is debited and D credited with ₹8,000.

options.text: D's Capital A/c Dr ₹8,000; To F's Capital A/c ₹8,000
options.explanation: The direction is reversed. D has the largest capital relative to his profit share, so the omission of interest cost HIM and benefited F; D must be credited.

options.text: F's Capital A/c Dr ₹16,000; To D's Capital A/c ₹16,000
options.explanation: This takes only one side of the statement — the extra profit each partner received — and forgets to set the interest each should have been given against it. The two columns must be netted.

options.text: D's Capital A/c Dr ₹40,000, E's Capital A/c Dr ₹32,000 and F's Capital A/c Dr ₹8,000; To Profit and Loss Adjustment A/c ₹80,000
options.explanation: This reopens the past year through an adjustment account and debits the partners with the interest they were owed. A past adjustment is settled by ONE net entry between the partners' capital accounts; the closed accounts are never reopened.

questions.sourceRef: Past adjustment: interest that should have been given, less extra profit already taken

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Past adjustments
questions.stem: G, H and I divided the profits EQUALLY for the two years ended 31 March 2026, whereas the deed required 5:3:2. The profits were ₹3,60,000 for 2024–25 and ₹4,80,000 for 2025–26. The single adjusting entry is:

options.text: G's Capital A/c Dr ₹1,40,000; To H's Capital A/c ₹28,000 and I's Capital A/c ₹1,12,000
options.explanation: The direction is reversed. G was entitled to the LARGEST share (5/10) but received only a third, so he was short-changed and must be credited, not debited.

options.text: H's Capital A/c Dr ₹28,000 and I's Capital A/c Dr ₹1,12,000; To G's Capital A/c ₹1,40,000
options.explanation: Correct. Total profit of the two years = ₹8,40,000. Correct shares (5:3:2) = G ₹4,20,000, H ₹2,52,000, I ₹1,68,000. Actual shares (equal) = ₹2,80,000 each. Differences: G short by ₹1,40,000; H over by ₹28,000; I over by ₹1,12,000. So H and I are debited and G credited.

options.text: H's Capital A/c Dr ₹16,000 and I's Capital A/c Dr ₹64,000; To G's Capital A/c ₹80,000
options.explanation: This corrects only 2025–26 and leaves 2024–25 uncorrected. Both years were divided wrongly, so the total of both must be restated.

options.text: G's Capital A/c Dr ₹1,12,000 and H's Capital A/c Dr ₹28,000; To I's Capital A/c ₹1,40,000
options.explanation: This applies the ratio in reverse as 2:3:5, making I the largest sharer. The deed's ratio is 5:3:2, with G first.

questions.sourceRef: Past adjustment for profits divided in the wrong ratio, both years taken together

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Goodwill — average profit method
questions.stem: A firm's profits for the last five years were: 2021–22 ₹2,40,000; 2022–23 ₹2,80,000; 2023–24 ₹3,20,000; 2024–25 ₹3,60,000 (including ₹20,000 profit on the sale of a delivery van); 2025–26 ₹3,00,000 (after charging a ₹40,000 loss of stock by fire, which is not expected to recur). Goodwill is to be valued at 2 years' purchase of the average profit. Goodwill is:

options.explanation: This averages the profits as reported, without adjusting for the abnormal items. Past profits must first be restated to normal, recurring earning power.

Correct. Adjusted profits: 2,40,000; 2,80,000; 3,20,000; 3,60,000 − 20,000 (non-recurring gain on sale of the van) = 3,40,000; 3,00,000 + 40,000 (abnormal fire loss added back) = 3,40,000. Total ₹15,20,000 ÷ 5 = ₹3,04,000 average. Goodwill = 3,04,000 × 2 = ₹6,08,000.

This applies both adjustments the wrong way round — adding the abnormal gain and deducting the abnormal loss. An abnormal GAIN inflates past profit and must come out; an abnormal LOSS depresses it and must be added back.
This is the adjusted average profit itself. The question asks for goodwill at 2 years' purchase, so it must still be multiplied by 2.

questions.sourceRef: Average profit method with adjustment for abnormal gains and losses

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Goodwill — weighted average
questions.stem: A firm's profits were: 2022–23 ₹1,80,000; 2023–24 ₹2,20,000; 2024–25 ₹2,60,000; 2025–26 ₹3,00,000. Because the business is growing, weights of 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively are to be used. Goodwill is valued at 3 years' purchase of the weighted average profit. Goodwill is:

options.explanation: This uses the SIMPLE average of ₹2,40,000. The question directs a weighted average, which pulls the figure up because the best years carry the heaviest weights.
This applies the weights in reverse (4, 3, 2, 1), giving the oldest and smallest profit the greatest influence. The heaviest weight belongs to the most recent year.
This is the weighted average profit itself, before applying the 3 years' purchase.

questions.sourceRef: Weighted average profit = total of (profit × weight) ÷ total of weights

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Goodwill — super profit method
questions.stem: The capital employed in a firm is ₹15,00,000 and the normal rate of return in that trade is 15%. The firm's adjusted average profit is ₹3,00,000. Goodwill is to be valued at 4 years' purchase of the super profit. Goodwill is:

options.explanation: This is 4 years' purchase of the AVERAGE profit of ₹3,00,000. The question asks for 4 years' purchase of the SUPER profit, which is only the excess over the normal return.
This capitalises the super profit (75,000 ÷ 0.15). That is a different method — the question specifies 4 years' purchase.
This is the super profit itself. It must still be multiplied by the 4 years' purchase.

questions.sourceRef: Super profit = adjusted average profit − (capital employed × normal rate of return)

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Goodwill — capitalisation
questions.stem: A firm's adjusted average profit is ₹4,20,000 and the normal rate of return is 14%. Its assets, excluding goodwill, are ₹36,00,000 and its outside liabilities are ₹9,00,000. Goodwill by the CAPITALISATION OF AVERAGE PROFIT method is:

options.explanation: Correct. Capital employed = 36,00,000 − 9,00,000 = ₹27,00,000. Capitalised value of the business = 4,20,000 ÷ 0.14 = ₹30,00,000. Goodwill = 30,00,000 − 27,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. (Cross-check by the other capitalisation route: super profit = 4,20,000 − 27,00,000 × 14% = ₹42,000, and 42,000 ÷ 0.14 = ₹3,00,000 — the two capitalisation methods always agree.)
This is the capitalised value of the whole business. Goodwill is only the EXCESS of that value over the capital actually employed.
This is the super profit (4,20,000 − 3,78,000). It has to be capitalised at 14%, or the capitalised value compared with capital employed, before it becomes goodwill.
This is the super profit taken at 3 years' purchase — a method the question did not ask for, and one whose number of years' purchase was never given.

questions.sourceRef: Goodwill = (average profit ÷ normal rate) − capital employed

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Goodwill — annuity method
questions.stem: A firm's super profit is ₹80,000 and is expected to continue for 5 years. The present value of an annuity of ₹1 for 5 years at 10% is 3.7908; the future value of an annuity of ₹1 for 5 years at 10% is 6.1051. Goodwill by the annuity method is:

options.explanation: This is the undiscounted total of five years' super profit. The annuity method exists precisely because ₹80,000 receivable in year 5 is worth less today than ₹80,000 received now.
This capitalises the super profit at 10% (80,000 ÷ 0.10), which assumes the super profit lasts for ever. The stem limits it to 5 years.

This uses the FUTURE value factor 6.1051. Goodwill is what the stream is worth today, so the PRESENT value factor is the one to use — and the answer must be less than the undiscounted ₹4,00,000, not more.
Correct. Goodwill = super profit × present-value annuity factor = 80,000 × 3.7908 = ₹3,03,264.

questions.sourceRef: Annuity method: goodwill = super profit × present value annuity factor

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Goodwill and AS 26
questions.stem: On the admission of a new partner, the old partners propose to pass the entry 'Goodwill A/c Dr ₹5,00,000; To Old Partners' Capital A/cs ₹5,00,000' so that the goodwill they built appears in the balance sheet. Is this correct?

options.text: Yes, provided the goodwill is written off against the partners' capitals within five years
options.explanation: Writing it off later does not cure the initial recognition. AS 26 bars the asset from being raised in the first place.

options.text: No — AS 26 permits only purchased goodwill to be recognised, so self-generated goodwill is adjusted through the partners' capital accounts instead
options.explanation: Correct. Goodwill can be recognised only where a consideration in money or money's worth has actually been paid for it. Goodwill the partners generated themselves has no cost and is never raised; on reconstitution it is adjusted directly between the gaining and the sacrificing partners' capital accounts.

options.text: Yes, because the partners have agreed a value and a partnership is free to value its own assets
options.explanation: Agreement between partners fixes the AMOUNT to be adjusted; it cannot override an accounting standard on whether an asset may be recognised at all.

options.text: No — goodwill may be raised only if it is written off immediately in the NEW profit-sharing ratio
options.explanation: This describes the pre-AS 26 'raise and write off' treatment. It is no longer accepted, and writing off in the new ratio would in any case shift value away from the sacrificing partners.

questions.sourceRef: AS 26 — only purchased goodwill is recognised

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Goodwill — capital employed
questions.stem: In computing goodwill by the super profit method, which of the following is EXCLUDED from capital employed?

options.text: Trade receivables, net of the provision for doubtful debts
options.explanation: Debtors are used in the business and are included at their realisable value.

options.text: Closing stock, because it will be sold in the following year
options.explanation: Stock is a trading asset employed in the business and is included.

options.text: Plant and machinery, because it is stated at written-down value rather than market value
options.explanation: Fixed assets used in the business are very much part of capital employed. If the question gives revalued figures, those are used.

options.text: Goodwill already appearing in the balance sheet, and non-trade investments
options.explanation: Correct. Capital employed means the capital used in EARNING the profit being measured. Existing goodwill is excluded so that goodwill is not counted twice; non-trade investments are excluded because their income is not part of the trading profit; and fictitious assets are excluded because they are not assets at all.

questions.sourceRef: Capital employed excludes goodwill, non-trade investments and fictitious assets

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Admission — new and sacrificing ratios
questions.stem: A and B share profits 5:3. C is admitted for a 1/4 share, which he acquires 1/8 from A and 1/8 from B. The new profit-sharing ratio of A, B and C is:

options.explanation: This leaves A and B at 5/8 and 3/8 and simply appends C's 2/8. The three shares then total 10/8 — more than the whole profit. C's share must come OUT of A's and B's.
This assumes A and B sacrifice in their old ratio 5:3 (A 5/8 × 3/4 = 15/32, B 9/32, C 8/32). The stem says each of them gives up 1/8, an EQUAL sacrifice, so the old-ratio assumption does not apply.
Correct. A = 5/8 − 1/8 = 4/8; B = 3/8 − 1/8 = 2/8; C = 1/8 + 1/8 = 2/8. The new ratio is 4 : 2 : 2, that is 2 : 1 : 1. The sacrificing ratio is 1/8 : 1/8 = 1 : 1.
This gives C only 1/8 while still taking 1/8 from each of A and B, so the shares do not add up to one. C acquires 1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4.

questions.sourceRef: New share = old share − sacrifice; sacrificing ratio = old ratio − new ratio

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Admission — premium for goodwill
questions.stem: P and Q share profits 3:2. R is admitted for a 1/5 share and brings ₹1,50,000 in cash as premium for goodwill, which is retained in the business. P and Q agree that they will share the remaining profits EQUALLY between themselves. The premium is credited:

options.text: Wholly to P — ₹1,50,000; Q receives nothing
options.explanation: Correct. New shares: R 1/5; P and Q take half of the remaining 4/5 each, so 2/5 each. Sacrifice = old − new: P = 3/5 − 2/5 = 1/5, Q = 2/5 − 2/5 = nil. Q gives up nothing, so the entire premium goes to P, the only sacrificing partner.
This shares the premium in the OLD ratio 3:2. The premium always follows the SACRIFICING ratio; here Q's sacrifice is zero, so he can receive nothing.
This shares the premium in P and Q's new mutual ratio of 1:1. A partner is compensated for what he GIVES UP, not for what he retains.
This reverses the old ratio. Even on the wrong principle the split would favour P, and on the right principle Q receives nothing at all.

questions.sourceRef: Premium for goodwill is credited in the sacrificing ratio, which may be nil for a partner

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Admission — premium paid privately
questions.stem: On admission, the incoming partner pays ₹2,00,000 as premium for goodwill DIRECTLY to the old partners in their private capacity, outside the firm. The entry in the firm's books is:

options.text: Cash A/c Dr ₹2,00,000; To Old Partners' Capital A/cs ₹2,00,000
options.explanation: No cash has come into the firm. The money passed privately between the partners, so the firm's cash book is untouched.

options.text: Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr ₹2,00,000; To Old Partners' Capital A/cs ₹2,00,000
options.explanation: There is no Premium for Goodwill Account to close, because none was ever opened — the firm never received the premium.

options.text: Goodwill A/c Dr ₹2,00,000; To Old Partners' Capital A/cs ₹2,00,000
options.explanation: This raises self-generated goodwill as an asset, which AS 26 does not permit, and it records a transaction the firm was not a party to.

options.text: No entry at all
options.explanation: Correct. A premium paid privately never enters the firm's books: the firm neither receives nor pays anything, and no asset or liability of the firm changes. The transaction is between the partners personally.

questions.sourceRef: Premium paid privately: no entry in the firm's books

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Admission — hidden goodwill
questions.stem: M and N share profits 3:2. After all revaluation and reserve adjustments their capitals are ₹6,00,000 and ₹4,00,000. O is admitted for a 1/5 share and brings ₹3,00,000 as capital but nothing for goodwill. The goodwill of the firm implied by O's capital is:

options.explanation: This is O's SHARE of the hidden goodwill (₹2,00,000 × 1/5). The question asks for the goodwill of the firm as a whole.
This is the total capital the OLD partners ought to have (₹15,00,000 − O's ₹3,00,000). It is a step in a capital-adjustment question, not the goodwill.
This deducts only the old partners' ₹10,00,000 from the implied total of ₹15,00,000, forgetting that O's own ₹3,00,000 is also part of the firm's actual capital.

Correct. O pays ₹3,00,000 for a 1/5 share, so he values the whole firm at 3,00,000 × 5 = ₹15,00,000. The firm's actual combined capital is 6,00,000 + 4,00,000 + 3,00,000 = ₹13,00,000. The difference, ₹2,00,000, is the hidden goodwill; O's share of it (₹40,000) is debited to his capital account and credited to M and N in their sacrificing ratio 3:2.

questions.sourceRef: Hidden goodwill = (new partner's capital × reciprocal of his share) − total adjusted capital

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Admission — Revaluation Account
questions.stem: X and Y share profits 7:3 and admit Z. On revaluation: stock of ₹2,40,000 is to be reduced by 10%; a provision for doubtful debts of ₹18,000 is to be created; machinery of ₹5,00,000 is to be appreciated by 12%; an unrecorded investment worth ₹35,000 is to be brought into the books; and an unrecorded electricity bill of ₹9,000 is to be provided for. X's share of the revaluation result is:

options.text: ₹30,800 credit
options.explanation: Correct. Credits: machinery 5,00,000 × 12% = ₹60,000 and unrecorded investment ₹35,000 = ₹95,000. Debits: stock 2,40,000 × 10% = ₹24,000, provision ₹18,000 and outstanding bill ₹9,000 = ₹51,000. Revaluation profit = 95,000 − 51,000 = ₹44,000, shared by the OLD partners in the OLD ratio 7:3 → X = 44,000 × 7/10 = ₹30,800.

options.text: ₹13,200 credit
options.explanation: This is Y's share — the 7:3 ratio has been applied the wrong way round.

options.text: ₹22,000 credit
options.explanation: This divides the ₹44,000 equally, or between three partners in some other way. Revaluation profit belongs to the OLD partners in their OLD ratio; the incoming partner takes no part in it.

options.text: ₹6,300 credit
options.explanation: This leaves the unrecorded investment of ₹35,000 out of the credits, reducing the revaluation profit to ₹9,000. An unrecorded ASSET brought into the books is a gain and must be credited.

questions.sourceRef: Revaluation profit or loss belongs to the old partners in the old ratio

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Admission — revaluation and reserves
questions.stem: On the admission of a new partner, the General Reserve standing in the balance sheet and the profit on revaluation are transferred:

options.text: To all partners including the incoming one, in the new profit-sharing ratio
options.explanation: Both items arose entirely before the new partner joined. Giving him a share would hand him value he did not help create and did not pay for.

options.text: To all partners including the incoming one, in the old profit-sharing ratio
options.explanation: The incoming partner has no share in the old ratio at all, so he cannot receive anything under it. This option is internally inconsistent.

options.text: To the old partners only, in the old profit-sharing ratio
options.explanation: Correct. Accumulated reserves and profits were earned, and the revaluation surplus accrued, while only the old partners were in the firm. Both are therefore credited to the OLD partners in their OLD ratio before the new partner's admission takes effect.

options.text: To the old partners only, in their sacrificing ratio
options.explanation: The sacrificing ratio governs the premium for GOODWILL. Reserves and revaluation results follow the old profit-sharing ratio, which is usually different.

questions.sourceRef: Reserves and revaluation results on admission: old partners, old ratio

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Admission — accumulated losses
questions.stem: The balance sheet of a firm being reconstituted on the admission of a partner shows an 'Advertisement Suspense Account' of ₹60,000 on the assets side. On admission it should be:

options.text: Carried forward unchanged, since it will be written off against future advertising revenue
options.explanation: It is a fictitious asset representing expenditure already incurred, not a cost recoverable from future revenue.

options.text: Written off by debiting the OLD partners' capital accounts in the OLD profit-sharing ratio
options.explanation: Correct. Advertisement Suspense is deferred expenditure — an accumulated LOSS that belongs to the period before the new partner joined. It is written off among the old partners in the old ratio, exactly as a debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account would be.

options.text: Written off by debiting all partners, including the new one, in the new ratio
options.explanation: The new partner had no part in incurring it and should not bear it.

options.text: Debited to the Revaluation Account along with the other adjustments
options.explanation: The Revaluation Account deals with restating assets and liabilities to fair values. A fictitious asset is not revalued — it is written off directly against the old partners' capitals.

questions.sourceRef: Accumulated losses and fictitious assets: written off to old partners in the old ratio

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Retirement — gaining ratio
questions.stem: A, B and C share profits 4:3:2. B retires and A and C agree to share future profits 5:3. The gaining ratio of A and C is:

options.explanation: This is simply the NEW ratio. The gain is the INCREASE in each partner's share, not the share itself.

Correct. A's gain = 5/8 − 4/9 = (45 − 32)/72 = 13/72. C's gain = 3/8 − 2/9 = (27 − 16)/72 = 11/72. Gaining ratio = 13 : 11. Note that A gains only a little more than C even though his share is much bigger.
This is the old ratio of the continuing partners (4:2). It would be the gaining ratio only if the question had NOT specified a new ratio.
The two gains have been swapped. A's share rises from 4/9 (0.444) to 5/8 (0.625), a gain of 13/72, which is the larger of the two.

questions.sourceRef: Gaining ratio = new ratio − old ratio

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Retirement — goodwill adjustment
questions.stem: P, Q and R share profits 3:2:1. Q retires, and P and R agree to share future profits 3:2. The goodwill of the firm is valued at ₹4,80,000. The correct adjusting entry is:

options.text: Goodwill A/c Dr ₹4,80,000; To P's, Q's and R's Capital A/cs in 3:2:1
options.explanation: This raises self-generated goodwill as an asset, which AS 26 forbids. Only an adjustment between capital accounts is permitted.

options.text: P's Capital A/c Dr ₹96,000 and R's Capital A/c Dr ₹64,000; To Q's Capital A/c ₹1,60,000
options.explanation: The total credited to Q is right, but it has been borne in the continuing partners' OLD ratio 3:1 (shown here as 3:2 of the amount). The burden follows the GAINING ratio.

options.text: P's Capital A/c Dr ₹80,000 and R's Capital A/c Dr ₹80,000; To Q's Capital A/c ₹1,60,000
options.explanation: This splits Q's goodwill equally. R gains far more than P on these figures, so he must bear more.

options.text: P's Capital A/c Dr ₹48,000 and R's Capital A/c Dr ₹1,12,000; To Q's Capital A/c ₹1,60,000

questions.sourceRef: Retiring partner's goodwill is borne by the gainers in the gaining ratio

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Retirement — hidden goodwill
questions.stem: S, T and U share profits 5:3:2. T retires. After revaluation and the transfer of reserves his capital account stands at ₹6,40,000, and the partners agree that he will be paid ₹7,60,000 in full settlement. The goodwill of the firm is:

options.explanation: This is T's SHARE of the goodwill, not the firm's goodwill. It must be grossed up by the reciprocal of his profit share.
This grosses up T's ₹1,20,000 by 10 instead of by 10/3. T's share of profits is 3/10, so the multiplier is 10/3, not 10.

Correct. The excess paid over the balance standing to T's credit is 7,60,000 − 6,40,000 = ₹1,20,000, and that excess IS T's share of goodwill. His share of profits is 3/10, so the firm's goodwill = 1,20,000 × 10/3 = ₹4,00,000.
This treats the whole settlement as goodwill. Most of that amount is simply T's own capital being returned to him.

questions.sourceRef: Hidden goodwill on retirement = (amount payable − capital balance) × reciprocal of his share

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Retirement — settlement
questions.stem: A retiring partner's balance is transferred to his Loan Account because the firm cannot pay him immediately. The deed and the partners are silent about interest. What interest is he entitled to?

options.text: 6% per annum, the rate the Indian Partnership Act supplies for money left with the firm
options.explanation: Correct. Once the balance is transferred to a loan account the retiring partner stands as a lender to the firm, and the Act's 6% p.a. rule for a partner's advance applies when nothing else is agreed. The loan appears as a liability in the balance sheet until it is discharged.

options.text: The same rate as the deed allowed on partners' capital while he was a partner
options.explanation: The deed's interest-on-capital clause governs partners' capital. He is no longer a partner, and his balance is no longer capital.

options.text: No interest, because the amount is payable on demand
options.explanation: The whole reason for a loan account is that payment is deferred. Deferring it without compensation would leave the firm using his money free of cost.

options.text: Interest at the rate the firm pays on its bank overdraft
options.explanation: There is no such rule. The Act supplies a fixed rate in the absence of agreement.

questions.sourceRef: Retiring partner's loan: 6% p.a. in the absence of agreement

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Death — profit to the date of death
questions.stem: K, L and M share profits 3:2:1. M dies on 30 June 2025 and the firm closes its books on 31 March. Sales for the year ended 31 March 2025 were ₹50,00,000 on which the profit was ₹6,00,000. Sales from 1 April 2025 to 30 June 2025 were ₹9,00,000. The deed requires the profit to the date of death to be estimated on the basis of turnover. M's share is:

options.explanation: Correct. Last year's rate of net profit on sales = 6,00,000 ÷ 50,00,000 = 12%. Profit for 1 April to 30 June 2025 = 9,00,000 × 12% = ₹1,08,000. M's share = 1,08,000 × 1/6 = ₹18,000.
This uses the TIME basis: 6,00,000 × 3/12 × 1/6 = ₹25,000. The deed specifies the turnover basis, and the two give different answers precisely because sales were not spread evenly.
This is the firm's whole profit for the three months. M is entitled only to his 1/6 share of it.
This takes M's share as 1/3. The ratio is 3:2:1, so M's share is 1/6.

readLink.label: Read: Profit to the date of death, §13 →

questions.sourceRef: Turnover basis: sales to date × last year's rate of net profit on sales × his share

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Death — executor's amount
questions.stem: A, B and C share profits 2:2:1. C dies on 30 September 2025 (the firm closes on 31 March). On that date his capital was ₹3,00,000; the General Reserve stood at ₹2,00,000; revaluation produced a LOSS of ₹50,000; the goodwill of the firm was valued at ₹5,00,000; C had drawn ₹40,000 up to the date of death; and his share of the current year's profit is to be credited on a time basis, last year's profit having been ₹3,60,000. The amount payable to C's executor is:

options.explanation: This omits C's share of goodwill (₹1,00,000). A deceased partner is entitled to his share of the firm's goodwill, borne by the continuing partners in their gaining ratio.
This ADDS the share of the revaluation loss instead of deducting it. A loss on revaluation reduces every partner's capital, including that of the deceased.
This adds back the ₹40,000 of drawings instead of deducting them. Drawings are money C had already taken and must reduce the amount still payable to his executor.

questions.sourceRef: Executor's amount = capital + reserves + revaluation + goodwill + profit to date − drawings

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Death — profit to the date of death
questions.stem: P, Q and R share profits 5:3:2. R dies on 31 August 2025 and the firm closes on 31 March. The deed provides that his share of the current year's profit be estimated on the AVERAGE PROFIT of the last three years, which were ₹4,20,000, ₹4,80,000 and ₹5,40,000. R's share of profit to the date of death is:

options.explanation: This gives R a full year's share of the average profit (4,80,000 × 2/10). He was a partner for only five of the twelve months.
This uses the LATEST year's profit of ₹5,40,000 rather than the three-year average the deed specifies.
This counts seven months instead of five. R died on 31 August 2025, five months after the year began on 1 April 2025.

readLink.label: Read: Profit to the date of death, §13 →

questions.sourceRef: Time basis on the average profit of the last three years

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Death — presentation
questions.stem: The deceased partner's share of profit from the beginning of the year to the date of death is credited to his capital account. What is debited?

options.text: The continuing partners' capital accounts, in their gaining ratio
options.explanation: The gaining ratio governs the GOODWILL adjustment on death, not the share of profit for the current period.

options.text: The Revaluation Account, along with the other adjustments made on the date of death
options.explanation: The Revaluation Account restates assets and liabilities. The current period's trading profit has nothing to do with it.

options.text: The Profit and Loss Suspense Account, which is later absorbed when the year's accounts are made up
options.explanation: Correct. The year's accounts are not yet drawn up on the date of death, so the estimated share is parked in a Profit and Loss Suspense Account. When the full year's Profit and Loss Account is finally prepared, that suspense balance is set off against the profit for the year.

options.text: The General Reserve, to the extent it is available
options.explanation: The reserve is a separate item, and the deceased partner's SHARE of it is credited to him in addition to his share of profit. It is not the source of the current period's profit.

questions.sourceRef: Share of profit to date of death is debited to Profit and Loss Suspense A/c

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · LLP — features
questions.stem: Which statement about a Limited Liability Partnership is CORRECT?

options.text: It is a partnership firm whose partners have agreed among themselves to limit their liability
options.explanation: Limited liability in an LLP comes from the statute, not from an agreement between partners. Partners of an ordinary firm cannot limit their liability to outsiders by private agreement.

options.text: Its partners are agents both of the LLP and of one another, exactly as in a partnership firm
options.explanation: A partner of an LLP is an agent of the LLP ALONE and not of the other partners. That is the feature which stops one partner's misconduct from reaching the others personally.

options.text: It is a body corporate with perpetual succession, and a change in its partners does not affect its existence, rights or liabilities
options.explanation: Correct. An LLP is a body corporate formed and incorporated under the LLP Act 2008 and is a legal entity separate from its partners. It has perpetual succession, so partners may come and go without disturbing the entity itself.

options.text: It must have at least seven partners, of whom at least two must be resident in India
options.explanation: An LLP needs a minimum of TWO partners, with no maximum. What it needs at least two of, both individuals with at least one resident in India, is DESIGNATED partners.

questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008 — body corporate, separate legal entity, perpetual succession

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · LLP — designated partners
questions.stem: Which statement about designated partners of an LLP is CORRECT?

options.text: Every partner of an LLP is automatically a designated partner
options.explanation: Designated partners are specifically named, in the incorporation document or as the LLP agreement provides. Ordinary partners are not designated partners by default.

options.text: A body corporate may be a designated partner provided it is registered in India
options.explanation: A body corporate may be a PARTNER of an LLP, but a designated partner must be an individual.

options.text: Designated partners are liable for all the debts of the LLP without limit
options.explanation: Their liability for the LLP's ordinary obligations is limited like any other partner's. What they carry is responsibility for compliance — including penalties for default in filings.

options.text: An LLP must have at least two designated partners, both individuals, of whom at least one must be resident in India, and they answer for the LLP's statutory compliances
options.explanation: Correct. The Act requires a minimum of two designated partners who are individuals, with at least one resident in India, and makes them responsible for doing all acts and things required to be done by the LLP in respect of compliance with the Act, including the annual filings.

questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008 — at least two designated partners, individuals, one resident in India

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Partnership firm vs LLP
questions.stem: Which of the following is a difference between a partnership firm and an LLP?

options.text: A partnership firm cannot own property in its own name, whereas an LLP can
options.explanation: Correct. A firm is not a separate legal person, so its property is held by the partners jointly and dealings are in the partners' names. An LLP is a body corporate and holds property, sues and is sued in its own name.

options.text: A partnership firm must be registered, whereas registration of an LLP is optional
options.explanation: It is the reverse. Registration of a firm is optional (though an unregistered firm cannot sue to enforce its contractual rights), while an LLP comes into existence only on incorporation with the Registrar.

options.text: Profits of a partnership firm are shared under the agreement, whereas an LLP must share profits equally
options.explanation: Both share profits as their agreement provides. Where the agreement is silent, each statute supplies default terms.

options.text: A partnership firm has no maximum number of partners, whereas an LLP is limited to fifty
options.explanation: This too is the reverse. The number of partners in a firm is capped by the rules under the Companies Act, while an LLP may have any number of partners.

questions.sourceRef: Firm: no separate legal entity; LLP: body corporate owning property in its own name

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · LLP accounts
questions.stem: Which statement about the accounts of an LLP is CORRECT?

options.text: An LLP may not maintain its books on the cash basis; only the accrual basis is permitted
options.explanation: An LLP may keep proper books of account on either the cash basis or the accrual basis.

options.text: An LLP must keep proper books of account at its registered office and file, each year, a Statement of Account and Solvency and an Annual Return with the Registrar
options.explanation: Correct. Those two annual filings, together with the requirement to maintain proper books at the registered office, are the compliance backbone of an LLP — and are exactly what a partnership firm does not have to do.

options.text: What partners bring into an LLP is called capital, and no separate term is used
options.explanation: What a partner brings into an LLP is his CONTRIBUTION, which may be in cash, in tangible or intangible property or in other benefits, with its monetary value stated in the accounts.

options.text: Every LLP must have its accounts audited, whatever its turnover or contribution
options.explanation: Audit is required only where turnover or contribution exceeds the limits prescribed under the LLP Rules; smaller LLPs are exempt.

questions.sourceRef: LLP Act 2008 — proper books, Statement of Account and Solvency, Annual Return

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Rules in the absence of a deed
questions.stem: A and B started a business together on 1 April 2025 but never executed a partnership deed. State the rules that will govern (a) the sharing of profits and losses, (b) remuneration to a working partner, (c) interest on capital, (d) interest on drawings, and (e) interest on a loan advanced by a partner beyond his agreed capital. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: (a) Profits and losses are shared EQUALLY between the partners, whatever the relative sizes of their capitals or of their contributions of effort (s.13(b))
(b) No partner is entitled to any remuneration — salary or commission — for taking part in the conduct of the business (s.13(a))
(c) No interest on capital is allowed; and even where a deed does allow it, such interest is payable only out of profits, so none is allowed in a loss year (s.13(c))
(d) No interest is charged on drawings — interest on drawings arises only from a provision in the deed
skeleton.citation: Rules in the absence of a deed

skeleton.point: (e) A partner who makes a payment or advance beyond the capital he agreed to subscribe is entitled to interest on it at 6% per annum; this interest is a CHARGE against profit and is allowed whether or not the firm earns a profit (s.13(d))

questions.sourceRef: Indian Partnership Act 1932, s.13

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Charge vs appropriation
questions.stem: Explain the distinction between a charge against profit and an appropriation of profit in partnership accounts, and classify each of the following, giving a reason: (i) interest on a partner's loan to the firm, (ii) interest on a partner's capital, (iii) rent payable to a partner for premises used by the firm, (iv) transfer to General Reserve. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: A charge against profit is an expense of the business: it is debited to the Profit and Loss Account, is deducted in arriving at net profit, and is allowed whether or not the firm makes a profit

An appropriation of profit is a distribution of profit already earned: it is debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and can be made only to the extent profit is available; if the available profit is insufficient, appropriations are allowed in the ratio of the amounts claimed
(i) Interest on a partner's loan is a CHARGE. In lending to the firm the partner deals with it as an outsider; the interest is payable even in a loss year, at 6% p.a. if the deed is silent
(ii) Interest on a partner's capital is an APPROPRIATION. It rewards the partner as an owner and, under s.13(c), is payable only out of profits
skeleton.citation: s.13(c); interest on capital as an appropriation

skeleton.point: (iii) Rent payable to a partner for his premises is a CHARGE. The partner acts as a landlord, and the rent is an ordinary business expense of occupying the premises
skeleton.citation: Rent to a partner — charge against profit

skeleton.point: (iv) A transfer to General Reserve is an APPROPRIATION. It sets aside profit already earned and cannot be made when there is no profit

questions.sourceRef: Charge vs appropriation classification

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Goodwill — nature and valuation
questions.stem: Explain what is meant by goodwill, state why self-generated goodwill is not recorded in the books of a firm, and describe the super profit and capitalisation methods of valuing it. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Goodwill is the value of a firm's reputation — the extra earning power that enables an established firm to earn more than a normal return on the capital it employs. It is an intangible asset arising from factors such as location, product quality, an established clientele, efficient management and length of existence

Under AS 26 only PURCHASED goodwill, for which a consideration in money or money's worth has been paid, may be recognised. Self-generated goodwill has no identifiable cost and is never raised in the books; on reconstitution it is adjusted through the partners' capital accounts instead

Super profit method: normal profit = capital employed × normal rate of return; super profit = adjusted average profit − normal profit; goodwill = super profit × the agreed number of years' purchase. If super profit is nil or negative the firm has no goodwill
Capitalisation of average profit: capitalised value of the business = adjusted average profit ÷ normal rate of return; goodwill = that capitalised value − capital employed
Capitalisation of super profit: goodwill = super profit ÷ normal rate of return. The two capitalisation routes always give the same figure, because normal profit is itself capital employed × the rate

Before any method is applied the past profits must be ADJUSTED to normal recurring earning power: abnormal losses and non-recurring expenses added back, abnormal and non-trading gains deducted, and future recurring costs (such as a manager's salary hitherto provided free) deducted

questions.sourceRef: Goodwill valuation methods and AS 26

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Admission of a partner
questions.stem: State, with reasons, the accounting treatment on the admission of a partner of (a) the sacrificing ratio, (b) a premium for goodwill brought in cash, (c) a premium paid privately to the old partners, (d) the profit on revaluation of assets and liabilities, and (e) the General Reserve appearing in the balance sheet. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: (a) Sacrificing ratio = old ratio − new ratio. It measures the share each old partner gives up so the new partner can have one, and it is the ratio in which the old partners are compensated. Where the question is silent, the old partners are taken to sacrifice in their old ratio

(b) A premium brought in cash is credited to a Premium for Goodwill Account, which is then transferred to the SACRIFICING partners' capital accounts in the sacrificing ratio — never in the old or the new ratio. No Goodwill Account is raised, because AS 26 does not permit self-generated goodwill to be recognised
(c) A premium paid privately to the old partners outside the firm requires NO ENTRY in the firm's books: the firm neither receives nor pays anything and none of its assets or liabilities changes
(d) The profit (or loss) on revaluation is transferred to the OLD partners' capital accounts in the OLD ratio, because the change in values accrued entirely while only they were partners

(e) The General Reserve, like any accumulated profit, is credited to the OLD partners in the OLD ratio before the admission takes effect; a debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account or an Advertisement Suspense Account is similarly debited to them
skeleton.citation: Reserves and accumulated profits on admission

questions.sourceRef: Admission of a partner — standard treatments

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Retirement and death of a partner
questions.stem: Distinguish between the accounting on the retirement of a partner and on the death of a partner, and list the items credited and debited in arriving at the amount payable to a deceased partner's executor. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Both are reconstitutions, not dissolutions: the continuing partners carry on, assets and liabilities are revalued, reserves and accumulated profits or losses are transferred to ALL partners including the outgoing one in the OLD ratio, and the outgoing partner's share of goodwill is borne by the gaining partners in the GAINING ratio
skeleton.citation: Common treatment on retirement and death

skeleton.point: Difference 1: on retirement the balance is settled with the retiring partner himself; on death it is transferred to the deceased partner's EXECUTOR (legal representative)

Difference 2: death occurs on a date within the accounting year, so the deceased is entitled to a share of the profit from the beginning of the year to the date of death, estimated on a TIME basis or a TURNOVER basis as the deed provides; this is debited to the Profit and Loss Suspense Account
skeleton.citation: Profit to the date of death

skeleton.point: Credits to the executor: capital balance; share of reserves and accumulated profits in the old ratio; share of the revaluation profit; share of goodwill; share of profit to the date of death; and interest on capital to that date if the deed provides for it
Debits to the executor: drawings up to the date of death; interest on those drawings; share of any revaluation loss; and share of accumulated losses or fictitious assets

Until it is discharged, the amount due to the executor (or the retiring partner's loan account) is shown as a liability in the balance sheet and carries interest at 6% p.a. where nothing else is agreed

questions.sourceRef: Retirement and death — comparison and executor's account

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Partnership and LLP · Partnership firm and LLP
questions.stem: State any five points of difference between a partnership firm governed by the Indian Partnership Act 1932 and a Limited Liability Partnership governed by the LLP Act 2008. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Legal status: a partnership firm is not a separate legal entity — the firm is merely a collective name for the partners — whereas an LLP is a BODY CORPORATE and a legal entity separate from its partners

Liability: partners of a firm have unlimited liability, joint and several, for the firm's debts, whereas a partner of an LLP is not personally liable merely by reason of being a partner; his exposure is limited to his agreed contribution

Perpetual succession: a firm has none — it is affected by the death, retirement or insolvency of a partner — whereas an LLP has perpetual succession and continues irrespective of changes among its partners

Registration and filings: registration of a firm is optional (though an unregistered firm cannot sue to enforce its contractual rights), while an LLP exists only on incorporation with the Registrar and must file an Annual Return and a Statement of Account and Solvency each year

Agency and management: a partner of a firm is an agent of the firm AND of the other partners, whereas a partner of an LLP is an agent of the LLP only; an LLP must in addition have at least two designated partners, both individuals, at least one resident in India

questions.sourceRef: Partnership firm vs LLP — statutory comparison
